bodyMarkdown:
## Before you start

Nothing beyond fractions. If you can see that $\dfrac{1}{4}$ and 25 percent are the same thing written two ways, you are ready.

## The idea in plain language

Percent means **per hundred**. That is the whole of the definition: 37 percent is 37 out of every 100, the way 'per hour' means 'for each hour'.

Picture a chocolate bar scored into 100 tiny squares. Taking 37 percent means taking 37 squares. Now here is the part that trips people up all through this topic: if I take 37 percent of **your** bar and 37 percent of a bar twice the size, I have taken the same percentage but a very different amount of chocolate. A percentage is meaningless until you know what it is a percentage **of**.

Almost every mistake in this topic is a mistake about that: the percentage was correct, but it was applied to the wrong bar.

## What is actually going on

Two habits make this topic easy, and they are worth more than any formula.

**Habit one: turn every percentage into a multiplier.** A 20 percent rise is $\times 1.2$. A 20 percent fall is $\times 0.8$. A 35 percent discount is $\times 0.65$. Once changes are multipliers you can chain them by multiplying, and the order stops mattering — which is exactly why a 10 percent rise followed by a 10 percent fall does not return you to where you started: $1.1 \times 0.9 = 0.99$, a 1 percent loss.

**Habit two: name the base.** Write down what the 100 percent refers to before you compute anything. 'Twenty percent more than B' has B as its base. 'Twenty percent of the total' has the total as its base. When a question changes base halfway through — and CAT questions do this deliberately — you will notice.

Learning a few fraction equivalents saves real seconds under time pressure, because they turn division into cancellation: $12.5\% = \dfrac{1}{8}$, $16\tfrac{2}{3}\% = \dfrac{1}{6}$, $33\tfrac{1}{3}\% = \dfrac{1}{3}$, $37.5\% = \dfrac{3}{8}$, $62.5\% = \dfrac{5}{8}$.

## Every question type you will meet

Each of these is a shape a question in this topic actually comes in. Learn to recognise the shape first — in a timed paper, picking the right method is most of the battle, and the arithmetic is the easy part.

### 1. Successive percentage changes

**Spot it when:** two or more changes applied one after another — 'increased by 20 percent, then decreased by 15 percent', or a price marked up then discounted.

1. Turn each change into a multiplier: a rise of $r\%$ is $\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{100}\right)$, a fall of $r\%$ is $\left(1 - \dfrac{r}{100}\right)$.
2. Multiply all the multipliers together.
3. Subtract 1 and multiply by 100 to read off the single net percentage change.

**Worked through:** Up 20 percent then down 15 percent gives $1.20 \times 0.85 = 1.02$, so a net rise of 2 percent — not the 5 percent you get by subtracting.

### 2. Working backwards to the original

**Spot it when:** the question gives you the value **after** a change and asks for the value before it. 'After a 15 percent discount a shirt costs Rs. 850. Find the marked price.'

1. Identify the multiplier that was applied.
2. Divide the final value by that multiplier. Do not subtract the percentage from the final value — the percentage was of the original, which is precisely the number you do not have yet.

**Worked through:** Rs. 850 after a 15 percent discount means $0.85 \times \text{MP} = 850$, so $\text{MP} = \dfrac{850}{0.85} = 1000$. Adding 15 percent to 850 would have given 977.50, which is wrong.

### 3. A is x percent more or less than B

**Spot it when:** a comparison between two quantities, usually asking for the reverse comparison: 'if A is 25 percent more than B, by what percent is B less than A?'

1. Set the **base of the given statement** to 100. In 'A is 25 percent more than B', B is the base, so B = 100 and A = 125.
2. Now compute the reverse comparison against its own base: B is less than A by $\dfrac{125 - 100}{125} \times 100$.

**Worked through:** $\dfrac{25}{125} \times 100 = 20$, so B is 20 percent less than A. The two percentages are different because the bases are different.

### 4. Price, consumption and expenditure

**Spot it when:** a price rises and the question asks by how much consumption must be cut so spending stays the same (or the other way round).

1. Remember that expenditure $=$ price $\times$ quantity, so if expenditure is fixed the two multipliers must multiply to 1.
2. If price becomes $\times p$, quantity must become $\times \dfrac{1}{p}$.
3. Convert that back into a percentage change.

**Worked through:** Price up 25 percent means $\times 1.25$, so quantity must be $\times \dfrac{1}{1.25} = 0.8$ — a 20 percent cut, not 25.

### 5. Pass marks and shortfalls

**Spot it when:** a candidate scores some marks, fails by a margin, and you are asked for the maximum marks or the pass percentage.

1. Write the pass mark two ways: as (score $+$ shortfall), and as (pass percentage $\times$ maximum marks).
2. Set them equal and solve for the unknown.

**Worked through:** Scoring 180 and failing by 20 in a 40 percent-pass exam means the pass mark is 200, so $0.40M = 200$ and $M = 500$.

### 6. Repeated growth over periods

**Spot it when:** a population, salary or value growing by the same percentage every year for several years.

1. This is one multiplier applied $n$ times: final $=$ initial $\times \left(1 + \dfrac{r}{100}\right)^n$.
2. For a decline, use $\left(1 - \dfrac{r}{100}\right)^n$.
3. If you are given the start and the end and asked for the rate, take the $n$th root.

**Worked through:** 10000 growing at 10 percent for 3 years reaches $10000 \times 1.1^3 = 13310$.

### 7. Percentage change in area or volume

**Spot it when:** a length, side or radius changes by a percentage and the question asks about the resulting area or volume.

1. Write the multiplier for the length.
2. Area depends on two lengths, so square the multiplier; volume depends on three, so cube it.
3. Convert back to a percentage.

**Worked through:** A side up 20 percent is $\times 1.2$, so area is $\times 1.2^2 = 1.44$ — a 44 percent increase, not 40.

## Check yourself

You are ready to start practising this topic when you can:

- Convert any percentage change into a multiplier without thinking about it.
- State what the base is before computing anything.
- Chain successive changes by multiplying, and recover the original by dividing.
- Convert between 'A is x percent more than B' and 'B is y percent less than A'.
- Handle the price-consumption-expenditure triangle in either direction.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: A shopkeeper raises the price of an item by 25 percent and then offers a 20 percent discount on the new price. What is the net percentage change in price?
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
Turn both changes into multipliers and chain them.

The rise is $\times 1.25$ and the discount is $\times 0.80$.

$1.25 \times 0.80 = 1.00$

The multiplier is exactly 1, so the price is back where it started: **no net change**.
workedExamples.altSolutionMarkdown: As fractions this is instant: a 25 percent rise multiplies by $\dfrac{5}{4}$ and a 20 percent discount by $\dfrac{4}{5}$. Those are reciprocals, so they cancel. Spotting reciprocal pairs like $\dfrac{5}{4}$ and $\dfrac{4}{5}$ saves the arithmetic entirely.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: After spending 30 percent of her salary on rent and 20 percent of the remainder on food, Nidhi is left with Rs. 22400. What is her salary?
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
Watch the base carefully: the 20 percent is of what is **left after rent**, not of the salary.

After rent she has $70\%$ of her salary, so a multiplier of $0.70$.

She then spends 20 percent of that, keeping 80 percent of it: another multiplier of $0.80$.

So what remains is $0.70 \times 0.80 = 0.56$ of her salary.

$0.56 \times S = 22400$, giving $S = \dfrac{22400}{0.56} = 40000$.

Her salary is **Rs. 40000**.
workedExamples.altSolutionMarkdown: The trap answer here is 50 percent — adding 30 and 20 as if both applied to the salary. They do not: the second percentage has a smaller base, which is why the true total spent is 44 percent, not 50.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: The price of rice rises by 20 percent. By what percentage must a family reduce its consumption so that its spending on rice is unchanged?
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
Spending $=$ price $\times$ quantity, and spending is to stay the same, so the two multipliers must multiply to 1.

Price is $\times 1.2$, so quantity must be $\times \dfrac{1}{1.2} = \dfrac{5}{6} \approx 0.8333$.

That is a fall of $1 - \dfrac{5}{6} = \dfrac{1}{6}$, which is $16\tfrac{2}{3}$ percent.

The family must cut consumption by **$16\tfrac{2}{3}$ percent**.
workedExamples.altSolutionMarkdown: This is the reverse-comparison idea again. A 20 percent rise is 'new is 20 percent more than old'; the cut needed is 'old is what percent less than new' — a different base, hence $16\tfrac{2}{3}$ rather than 20.

formulaCards.title: Successive changes
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: Net multiplier $= \left(1 + \dfrac{a}{100}\right)\left(1 + \dfrac{b}{100}\right)$, using a negative value for a decrease.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: Up 10 then down 10 gives $1.1 \times 0.9 = 0.99$: a 1 percent net fall.

formulaCards.title: Reverse comparison
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: If A is $x\%$ more than B, then B is $\dfrac{100x}{100 + x}\%$ less than A. If A is $x\%$ less than B, then B is $\dfrac{100x}{100 - x}\%$ more than A.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: A is 25 percent more than B, so B is $\dfrac{2500}{125} = 20$ percent less than A.

formulaCards.title: Fixed expenditure
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: Price $\times$ quantity is constant, so a price multiplier of $p$ needs a quantity multiplier of $\dfrac{1}{p}$.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: Price up 25 percent needs consumption down 20 percent.

formulaCards.title: Useful fraction equivalents
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: $37.5\%$ of 64 is $\dfrac{3}{8} \times 64 = 24$, faster than multiplying by 0.375.

commonTraps: Adding successive percentages instead of multiplying the multipliers. Up 20 then up 30 is a 56 percent rise, not 50.
Applying the percentage to the final value when the question asks for the original. Always divide by the multiplier, never subtract.
Losing track of the base when a question says 'of the remainder' — that is a new, smaller base.
Assuming a rise and a fall of the same percentage cancel. They never do; the result is always a small net loss.
Answering with the change when the question asked for the final value, or the other way round.
Treating a percentage-point difference as a percentage change. Going from 20 percent to 25 percent is 5 percentage points, but a 25 percent increase.
